Chicago Pile-1, the world's first artificial nuclear reactor, achieved criticality on December 2, 1942, under the University of Chicago's football stands.
Uranium-235 has a half-life of about 704 million years, while uranium-238 lasts about 4.47 billion years — roughly the age of the Earth.
Natural uranium is only about 0.7% U-235; most reactor fuel is enriched to around 3–5% U-235.
The blue glow in reactor pools is Cherenkov radiation, produced when charged particles travel faster than light does in water.
About 2 billion years ago, natural nuclear reactors ran on their own in uranium deposits at Oklo, Gabon.
Technetium-99m is the most widely used medical isotope, used in tens of millions of diagnostic scans every year.
Fission of one uranium-235 nucleus releases about 200 MeV of energy — millions of times more than a typical chemical reaction.
The Sun fuses roughly 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second.
Marie Curie is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics (1903) and chemistry (1911).
Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 when uranium salts fogged photographic plates kept in a drawer.
The sievert (Sv) measures the biological effect of radiation; the average person receives about 3 mSv a year from natural background sources.
Bananas contain potassium-40, a naturally radioactive isotope — which is where the informal 'banana equivalent dose' comes from.
The USS Nautilus, launched in 1954, was the world's first nuclear-powered submarine.
Obninsk in the Soviet Union became the first nuclear power plant to supply electricity to a grid, in 1954.
Voyager 1 and 2 are powered by radioisotope thermoelectric generators that turn heat from plutonium-238 decay into electricity.
Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch gave the first theoretical explanation of nuclear fission in 1939.
Neutrons were discovered by James Chadwick in 1932, opening the door to nuclear chain reactions.
Control rods often contain neutron-absorbing materials such as boron, cadmium, or hafnium to slow or stop the chain reaction.
In a pressurized water reactor, the primary coolant is kept at very high pressure so it stays liquid well above 300 °C.
Deuterium–tritium fusion is the reaction most fusion reactor designs, including ITER, plan to use.
Fission products are intensely radioactive at first, but most of their radioactivity decays away within the first few hundred years.
Smoke detectors commonly use a tiny amount of americium-241 to detect smoke particles.
Carbon-14 dating works because C-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years.
Ernest Rutherford's gold foil experiment in 1909–1911 revealed that atoms have a small, dense nucleus.
Enrico Fermi led the team that built Chicago Pile-1 and won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on neutron-induced reactions.
A Geiger–Müller tube detects ionizing radiation when a particle ionizes the gas inside it and triggers a pulse — the famous 'click'.
Alpha particles can be stopped by a sheet of paper, beta particles by aluminium, and gamma rays need dense materials like lead or thick concrete.
Thorium is about three to four times more abundant in Earth's crust than uranium and is being studied as a nuclear fuel.
Small modular reactors (SMRs) are designed to be factory-built and smaller than traditional plants, typically up to about 300 MWe.
Heavy water (D₂O) is used as a moderator in CANDU reactors, allowing them to run on natural, unenriched uranium.
